questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: detect which of the rhetorical situation's three questions a piece leaves open
questions.stem: A short piece runs: 'On Tuesday the council voted to close the footbridge for six months. The repair bill for the timber deck falls due in August. Residents who used the route to reach the bus interchange have not been told how they will get to work in the meantime.' Which of the rhetorical situation's three questions does this piece leave unanswered?

options.text: What the writer wants the reader to do about the closure
Who the writer is speaking to and for
options.misconception: confuses the residents mentioned with the audience the piece never addresses

options.text: What makes the matter urgent at this moment
options.misconception: confuses the topic of the piece with the situation that makes it timely

options.text: How much the repair itself is likely to cost
options.misconception: turns a missing element of the situation into a missing figure

questions.explanation: A rhetorical situation answers who is speaking, to whom, and what is at stake now. This piece is clear on two counts: residents are the people concerned, and the vote and the August bill supply the urgency. What it never supplies is a request. It describes the closure, the bill and the silence about travel, and then stops, so a reader finishes informed and unasked, which is why the unanswered question is the one about what should happen next.
questions.hint: Look for an instruction to the reader anywhere in the three sentences.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: match the instructions in a brief to the elements of a rhetorical situation
questions.stem: A brief for a newsletter piece says: 'Write for the readers of the parish newsletter, who already follow this argument. Keep it to four hundred words. Set it for the morning of the vote.' Which two elements of the rhetorical situation does the brief fix?

options.text: The audience and the context in which the piece appears
The audience and the purpose the piece is meant to serve
options.misconception: reads a statement about readers as though it stated what the piece should achieve

options.text: The purpose and the context, with the audience left open
options.misconception: ignores the clause that names exactly who the readers are

options.text: The context and the register, with no audience named at all
options.misconception: counts a word limit as a statement of rhetorical situation

questions.explanation: The brief pins two things down in plain words. 'For the readers of the parish newsletter, who already follow this argument' fixes the audience, including how much background the piece may assume, and 'the morning of the vote' fixes the context, which decides what can still be acted on. The purpose is never stated: nothing says whether the piece should persuade, inform or simply report, and the four hundred words is a length instruction rather than part of the situation.
questions.hint: Mark the clause that names people and the clause that names a moment.

questions.learningObjective: narrow an overbroad claim without withdrawing it
questions.stem: A draft says: 'Every teenager who uses a phone spends more than two hours a day on it.' Which revision narrows the claim to what the evidence could support?

options.text: Teenagers who use a phone for messaging report at least two hours a day on it
No teenager should spend more than two hours a day on a phone
options.misconception: turns a measured claim into an endorsement the original never made

options.text: No teenager spends more than two hours a day on a phone
options.misconception: denies the original claim outright instead of limiting its reach

options.text: Phones should be kept out of bedrooms after nine in the evening
options.misconception: substitutes a different proposal for the claim being narrowed

questions.explanation: Narrowing means holding the measurement and shrinking the population it is asserted of, which is what the first revision does: it keeps the two hours, adds the qualifier 'report', and limits the claim to teenagers who use a phone for messaging. Option B smuggles in a judgment about how the time should be spent, which no measurement in the draft can settle, and option C simply contradicts the draft. Option D argues for a rule, which is a different piece of work from fixing an overbroad sentence.
questions.hint: Look for the revision that keeps the figure and cuts the reach.

questions.learningObjective: recognise the ordering that makes a paragraph a problem and solution account
questions.stem: Which sequence of content is the one a problem and solution paragraph is built on?

options.text: The problem and its scale, its cause, the remedy, then what changes
The remedy first, the problem second, the cause of it last
options.misconception: reverses the order without giving a reason a reader could follow

options.text: The problem, the remedy, the cause, then the scale of the problem
options.misconception: puts the remedy between the problem and the cause that explains it

options.text: The cause, the problem it produces, the scale, then the remedy
options.misconception: opens on a cause where the paragraph must open on the problem

questions.explanation: A problem and solution paragraph earns its ending by establishing the problem first, sizing it so the reader can weigh the remedy, and only then supplying the remedy with the change it is expected to make. Option B hides the problem until second place and gives no purchase at all. Option C offers help before telling the reader what caused the difficulty, which is the diagnosis a solution needs. Option D is a cause and effect account of the same material rather than a proposal, since it never reaches a remedy until the end and never links it to the problem's scale.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader must already know before the remedy makes sense.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name the condition a candidate thesis fails
questions.stem: A draft opens with: 'Public libraries in this county remain open on Saturdays.' The writer says this sentence is the thesis. Which condition of a usable thesis does it fail?

options.text: A thesis must be contestable, and this one can only be confirmed
A thesis must name a date, and this sentence gives no year
options.misconception: demands a calendar detail that a thesis never has to carry

options.text: A thesis must state its evidence, and this sentence cites none
options.misconception: asks the thesis to do the work the body of the essay is for

options.text: A thesis must be one clause, and this sentence runs to eight words
options.misconception: objects to the length of a sentence rather than to what it claims

questions.explanation: A thesis commits the writer to something a reader could reasonably dispute, which is what makes the rest of the essay an argument rather than a description. The opening sentence commits to nothing contestable: a reader can go and see whether the libraries are open, so the sentence can only be confirmed. That is why it makes a poor thesis, and it explains the deeper problem, which is that an essay built on it would be reporting rather than arguing.
questions.hint: Ask whether a reader could disagree with the sentence and give reasons.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the sentence a paragraph's other sentences elaborate
questions.stem: A paragraph reads: 'That figure covers only two of the four terminals at the port. The other two are leased, and their volumes are reported by the operator rather than by us. When the operator's figures arrive, the total will be higher than the number quoted today. Until then, that number should be read as a floor rather than a measure.' Which sentence controls the paragraph?

options.text: That figure covers only two of the four terminals at the port
The other two are leased, and their volumes are reported by the operator
options.misconception: picks the sentence that supplies supporting detail rather than the limit being supported

options.text: Until then, that number should be read as a floor rather than a measure
options.misconception: picks the last sentence, which acts on the paragraph's point rather than stating it

options.text: When the operator's figures arrive, the total will be higher than today
options.misconception: picks a prediction about a future figure, which the other sentences qualify

questions.explanation: The controlling sentence is the one the rest of the paragraph exists to make good, and here the opening claim is that the figure is partial. The next two sentences say why, naming the two leased terminals and the operator who reports them, and the last sentence draws the consequence, that the quoted number is a floor. The test that decides it is coverage: remove the first sentence and the other three lose their subject, whereas remove the last and the paragraph still stands, because the last is what the writer wants done with the point.
questions.hint: Try deleting each sentence and see which one the others need.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: choose the connective that states the actual relation between two sentences
questions.stem: A draft joins two sentences with a blank: 'The lane is narrow at the pinch point by the depot. ___ the depot's lorries cross it twice in every shift, widening the lane there would cost more than it saves.' Which connective states the relation the second sentence actually bears to the first?

options.text: Because
Although
options.misconception: reads the cost comparison as a concession that works against the first sentence

options.text: For example
options.misconception: treats the lorry crossings as one instance of a narrow lane rather than its reason

options.text: So that
options.misconception: reverses the direction of the relation, making the cost the cause and the lane the result

questions.explanation: The second sentence explains why the first sentence's consequence follows: the lorries crossing twice a shift are the reason the widening would cost more than it saves, and 'because' is the connective that says so. 'Although' would announce a concession running against the first clause, and the cost comparison does not work that way. 'For example' would make the lorry crossings an instance of narrowness rather than its cause, and 'so' would run the reasoning backwards, making the cost the explanation for the lane's shape.
questions.hint: Ask which sentence answers the why-question raised by the other.

questions.learningObjective: select a sentence that paraphrases a finding in the writer's own words and names whose finding it is
questions.stem: A writer needs to use a survey finding: in one county, sixty-two per cent of commuters said they would cycle more if a protected lane existed. Which sentence reports it in the writer's own words and names whose finding it is?

options.text: Sixty-two per cent of commuters in one county said they would cycle more if a protected lane existed, according to the county's own transport survey
Sixty-two per cent of commuters in one county said they would cycle more if a protected lane existed
options.misconception: leaves the finding unattributed, so no reader can check who asked whom

options.text: Researchers have found that protected lanes change how people travel, with most commuters willing to cycle
options.misconception: reaches from stated willingness to a claim about behaviour the finding never covers

options.text: Sixty-two per cent of commuters in one county said they would cycle more, a figure repeated in several national papers
options.misconception: offers repeated publication as though repetition confirmed the finding

questions.explanation: A paraphrased finding has to keep two things from the source: what was asked, and who found it, and the first sentence does both while running the number into the writer's own sentence. Option B is the same words with the attribution stripped away, which leaves a reader unable to check anything. Option C quietly converts a stated willingness into a claim about how people actually travel, which is the overreach a paraphrase most often hides. Option D leans on repetition in the press, and repeated publication is not a second source.
questions.hint: Check that the sentence says what was asked and who found it.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name a boundary fault and choose a repair that preserves both clauses
questions.stem: A draft contains one sentence: 'The shared path was rebuilt in 2019, it has never flooded since.' First name the fault, then choose the repair that keeps both facts and their relation.

options.text: A comma splice, repaired by giving the second clause its own sentence
A comma splice, repaired by dropping the comma and adding the word and
options.misconception: believes a single subject with a compound predicate needs a semicolon or a new sentence

options.text: A run-on, repaired by deleting the comma after the year
options.misconception: calls the fault a run-on, which would need the comma removed and the clauses run on

options.text: A fragment, repaired by attaching the second clause to the first
options.misconception: treats a clause with its own subject and verb as an incomplete piece

Splitting the sentence keeps both facts and the time order between them, which is the relation the comma was failing to signal. Option B's repair would produce one subject with a compound predicate, which is not the structure the draft has, and option D misreads a complete clause as a fragment.
questions.hint: Check whether each half has its own subject and its own verb.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of an introduction that begins with a definition
questions.stem: A writer plans an essay that opens by defining a term the reader will not know. Put the four moves in the order that introduction needs.

options.text: State the thesis, so the reader knows what the term is being used to argue
options.misconception: leads with a conclusion the reader has no means of understanding yet

options.text: Name the term, so the reader has a word to hold on to
options.misconception: starts with an assertion that depends on the term being named first

options.text: Give a case the definition covers, so it is not left abstract
options.misconception: supplies illustration before the reader has been given the word

options.text: Show what the term does not settle, so the reader feels the need for a claim
options.misconception: reaches the limits of a term before the term has been given

questions.explanation: An opening definition earns its place only if the reader can use it, which takes three steps before the thesis. The word comes first, because nothing else can be said about a term the reader has never met. A case then shows the term doing work, and the limit follows, since a reader who has seen both an instance and the boundary of a definition is ready to hear what needs arguing. Placing the thesis at the end means the reader meets the claim already holding the tools to test it, which is why the other orders ask for judgement before they supply it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs before the thesis can be checked.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: recognise the ordering that makes a paragraph a cause and effect account
questions.stem: Which sequence of content is the one a cause and effect paragraph is built on?

options.text: The cause, the mechanism it sets off, the effect, and the evidence
The effect, the cause behind it, then a second effect it does not explain
options.misconception: leaves the paragraph with an effect the account never accounts for

options.text: The cause, the effect, the mechanism, and the evidence for it
options.misconception: separates a mechanism from the cause that sets it in motion

options.text: The evidence, the cause, the mechanism, and the effect last
options.misconception: opens on data where a cause and effect account opens on the process

questions.explanation: A cause and effect paragraph earns each step: the cause gives the reader something to follow, the mechanism shows how it works rather than asserting that it does, the effect states what came of it, and the evidence lets the reader check the claim. Option B sets out the same material backwards and then adds an outcome the earlier steps never produce, so the paragraph ends up explaining nothing. Option C puts the effect before the mechanism, which is the answer to a why-question, and option D asks the reader to hold figures in mind before knowing what they are figures of.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader must know before the next step makes sense.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: state what a counterargument section must contain before it can answer anything
questions.stem: A draft's counterargument section reads: 'Some people disagree with the parking changes. Parking changes are controversial. Not everyone agrees with parking changes. For these reasons, the changes should be kept.' What has the section failed to do?

options.text: State what those people say, in a form the writer can answer
Cite a source for the opposition, which the section has none of
options.misconception: demands a citation the section was never required to carry

options.text: Concede the opposition outright, which the section refuses to do
options.misconception: supposes that answering an objection means granting it

options.text: Move the objection to the opening, which is where it belongs
options.misconception: argues about the section's position instead of its content

questions.explanation: Three sentences saying that people disagree are still zero sentences of disagreement: the reader never learns the reason, so there is nothing for the writer to answer and the closing 'for these reasons' has no reasons to point back to. What the section needs is the opposing claim and the reason behind it, stated well enough that someone who holds it would recognise it. Option B makes a citation the requirement, which it is not, and option D treats placement as the fault when the problem is that the section says nothing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: describe what a concession gains and the ground it gives up
questions.stem: A writer arguing for a library closure says: 'The library is a comfort to some people, and I would not want it taken from them. All the same, it costs more to run than it earns, and so it should close.' What has the concession done, and what has it risked?

options.text: It granted a real value, then moved the dispute to cost
It denied that anyone is comforted, then reversed the denial
options.misconception: reads the concession as a denial followed by a change

options.text: It gave up the cost figure in exchange for the comfort it granted
options.misconception: supposes the concession trades a figure rather than a value

options.text: It conceded the whole case, since naming a value admits the library's worth
options.misconception: treats naming a value as though it were abandoning the claim

questions.explanation: The concession does real work: it grants that the library is worth something to people, which makes the writer sound fair and hands the dispute to a question about money that can be checked. The risk is that it grants the opponent's premise as well. Once comfort and attachment are conceded as real, closing the building looks less like a correction of waste and more like a decision to take something away, and the cost argument has to work harder than it would have. Option D names that risk but states it as though the concession had already lost the case.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer has admitted, and what that admission makes harder later.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a conclusion that restates from one that carries the claim outward
questions.stem: Draft A ends: 'So the shelter should be built, the money is set aside, and the council votes in March.' Draft B ends: 'So the shelter should be built. If it is, the queue at that gate belongs to people who now stand in the rain instead.' Which draft opens outward, and what does that move do?

options.text: Draft B, which carries the claim out to what it means for others
Draft A, which gives the reader the decision and the date again
options.misconception: counts a summary of the decision as an opening outward

options.text: Draft B, because it repeats the claim before adding to it
options.misconception: locates the outward move in the restatement rather than in the consequence

options.text: Draft A, because naming the date gives the reader something to act on
options.misconception: treats a logistics detail as a consequence for other people

questions.explanation: Opening outward means leaving the writer's own decision behind and following the claim out into the world, which is what the last sentence of Draft B does by naming the people the queue belongs to. A conclusion that restates, as Draft A does, leaves the reader exactly where the argument began, holding the same decision and the same date. The outward move is not longer and it is not more emphatic; it changes the subject of the final sentence from a matter of process to a matter of consequence.
questions.hint: Ask whose consequence the last sentence is about.

questions.learningObjective: repair a modifier that has no subject to attach to
questions.stem: A draft sentence reads: 'Handing the keys back on Friday, the flat was cleaned once more than the inventory required.' Which repair is both grammatical and faithful to what the writer meant?

Delete the opening phrase and keep the flat was cleaned once more than required

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify the effect a deliberate fragment produces
questions.stem: A passage reads: 'The council met for three hours. Eleven of those hours went on the barrier debate. Three minutes on the barrier. Then the vote.' What is the fragment doing here that a complete sentence would not do?

options.text: It shrinks an hour of debate to three minutes by ending the thought early
It is a fault, since a sentence in this register needs a main verb
options.misconception: applies a rule of finished prose to a deliberate break

options.text: It introduces the vote, so it works as the paragraph's topic sentence
options.misconception: reads a rhythmical break as a controlling idea

options.text: It shows irritation, which the following vote then confirms
options.misconception: loads the fragment with a judgment the passage states nowhere

questions.learningObjective: identify which noun a modifier can attach to
questions.stem: A sentence reads: 'The report that the auditor commissioned reached the committee before the deadline that the chair had set for the summary.' What can a reader not settle from this sentence alone?

Whether the auditor commissioned the report or the committee
options.misconception: makes the referent of commissioned the trouble, though both are named

options.text: Whether the report reached the committee or the summary did

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of a conclusion that does more than restate
questions.stem: A writer is closing an essay on a new footbridge. Put the four moves in the order a conclusion needs when it is to do more than repeat the argument.

options.text: Say what follows from the claim for someone other than the writer
options.misconception: opens outward before the reader has been reminded what the claim was

options.text: Restate the claim in words that show the reasoning behind it
options.misconception: leads with a consequence the reader has not been given the claim for

options.text: Narrow the claim, so the reader knows how far it reaches
options.misconception: fixes the reach of a claim that has not yet been restated

options.text: End on the limit of the evidence rather than on a fresh topic
options.misconception: closes by introducing something the essay has not argued

questions.explanation: A conclusion earns its length by doing four things in order. The claim comes first in new words, so the reader is reminded of what was argued, and the narrowing follows, because a reader who has just been handed a claim needs to know how far it holds before being asked to feel anything about it. Only then can the writer carry it outward to other people, and the limit comes last, since a hedge placed at the end of a sequence that has already broadened reads as an afterthought. Reversing any two of these steps asks the reader to accept a claim, or a feeling, before the material to judge it has arrived.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader needs in hand before the outward move can land.

questions.learningObjective: identify the population a share of complaints is drawn from
questions.stem: A brief says: 'Of the 4,100 complaints received last year, 22 per cent concerned bus frequency, and the total rose 8 per cent on the year before.' What still keeps a reader from weighing it?

options.misconception: demands a breakdown the brief's purpose did not need

questions.learningObjective: identify what a mid-sentence tense change costs and repair it
questions.stem: A draft reads: 'The clerk lists three payments, and then she explains that the second was never authorised. Her colleague says the form was signed.' First say what the tense shift costs, then give the repair.

questions.learningObjective: sequence the moves of an introduction built around a quotation
questions.stem: A writer plans an essay that opens with a sentence of their own used as a frame. Put the four moves in the order the introduction needs.

options.text: Gloss the quotation in a sentence of your own
options.misconception: explains a quotation the reader has not been given

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify why a thesis commits the writer to nothing testable
questions.stem: A draft's thesis reads: 'Technology has changed society.' What makes it hard to build an essay on?

options.misconception: judges the length of a sentence rather than its reach

options.text: It names two things, so the essay would need two introductions
options.misconception: counts the nouns the sentence happens to contain

options.misconception: insists on a tense rule that theses do not follow

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: identify what a formulaic close claims and what it withholds
questions.stem: A letter ends: 'I am sure you will give this your serious consideration.' What does that closing line do, and what does it leave out?

It states the reader's duty, which makes the request a moral one
options.misconception: reads a courtesy as an obligation

options.text: It thanks the reader in advance for a decision already taken
options.misconception: supposes a decision the sentence does not report

options.text: It ends on borrowed wording, which leaves the letter's purpose open
options.misconception: calls a set phrase a quotation

questions.explanation: The sentence puts the decision in the reader's mouth and calls it a certainty, so the letter never actually asks for anything or says what would count as a good outcome. questions.learningObjective: identify a ratio whose two numbers are counted over different spans
questions.stem: A brief says: 'Complaints now run at one for every two hundred riders, which is four times the rate of a year ago.' What keeps a reader from weighing that?

The word riders is not defined, and the brief should define it
options.misconception: asks for a definition where the periods disagree

options.text: Four times is too large a change to happen in a single year
options.misconception: judges the size of a change the brief never checks

options.text: No source is given for the number of complaints
options.misconception: demands attribution where the arithmetic is the fault

questions.explanation: A rate only means something when both of its numbers cover the same stretch of time, and riders is naturally a year's total while complaints, as briefs report them, is usually a month. questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name the problems in a short paragraph and state a claim that could be argued
questions.stem: A report reads: 'Enrolment in evening classes has fallen by a third since the new fees were introduced. Clearly, students have decided that evening study is not worth the money, and anyone who disagrees is out of touch with how hard students work.' In three to four sentences, name the two problems with the paragraph and rewrite the claim so it could be argued.

answer.exemplar: The first problem is that the fall in enrolment is treated as proof of a motive, when a rise in fees and a fall in numbers happening together leaves open the students who stopped coming for reasons of work, transport or timetables. The second problem is the closing clause, which dismisses anyone who disagrees instead of naming what such a reader would have to show. A arguable version would keep the fees as the focus, narrow the claim to what the figures bear on, and say what would settle it, such as the fees for comparable evening courses elsewhere.

questions.explanation: The two problems are of different kinds, so an answer that treats them as one will be thin. One is about evidence, where a correlation has been read as a decision made by students, and the other is about the treatment of opponents, where disagreement is recast as ignorance. A strong answer names both, keeps the writer's real concern, which is that evening classes are not being taken up, and gives a version of the claim that a reader could confirm or deny with figures rather than with agreement.
questions.hint: One problem is in what the fall is taken to show, the other in the last clause.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: name an ambiguous referent, show its cost, and fix it
questions.stem: A sentence reads: 'The delivery of the new signs, which were made by a firm in the next county, was delayed by a shortage of materials, which affected the whole region.' In three to four sentences, name what a reader cannot settle, show what each reading would mean, and fix the sentence.

answer.exemplar: The first which can attach either to the signs or to the delivery, so a reader cannot tell whether the firm in the next county made the signs or arranged the delivery, which is a different supplier altogether. The second which most naturally attaches to the shortage, but can also be read as attaching to the delay, and on that reading the delay affected the region while the shortage was local. The fix is to close the first relative clause with a comma and repeat the noun at the second, so that the firm is said to have made the signs and the shortage is said to be the thing that reached the whole region.

questions.explanation: Two relative clauses in one sentence, and a reader has to guess twice, which is why the sentence is harder to follow than its length suggests. The cost of the first ambiguity is commercial, since making the signs and delivering them are different jobs done by different firms, and the cost of the second is factual, since a shortage with regional reach and a delay with regional reach are different claims. A good answer identifies both attachment points, gives the two readings for at least one, and repairs the sentence with a comma or a repeated noun rather than by deleting the information.
questions.hint: Find each which and list the nouns it could attach to.
